bc_east_kootenay.blurb: East Kootenay covers the valley of southeastern British Columbia that lies between the Rocky Mountains to the east and the Purcell Mountains to the west, with Cranbrook as its biggest town. Sport climbing leads, mostly from 5.10 to 5.12 with a handful of moderates and a few 5.13s, and a large bouldering side runs from V0 up to about V6. Trad is a small minority, and there is a lone ice line. The best-known sport routes cluster at a few crags near Cranbrook. For bouldering, one zone near Kimberley offers steep quartzite on a talus slope, with slopers, big incuts and landings that have been built up.

or_carver.blurb: Carver lies near Gresham, a short drive from downtown Portland. It is mainly a bouldering area: hundreds of problems are scattered across a talus hillside below a single cliff band roughly 80 feet tall. Most boulder problems fall between V0 and V5, with a tail of harder ones up to V10 and beyond, and plenty of low-ball lines alongside a few taller, better-quality blocks. The cliff above adds roughly equal numbers of sport and trad routes, mostly from 5.9 to 5.12, plus a single top-rope line. Summer weekends and evenings are popular here. The two main parts are Carver Bouldering and Carver Cliff.

wa_mt_washington_2.blurb: Mt Washington is one of the three main climbing zones at Exit 38, off I-90 east of Seattle near North Bend. It is mainly a sport area, with most routes between 5.10 and 5.12, a good number of easier ones, and a small amount of bouldering and trad. The rock is metamorphosed andesite, often slightly overhanging and ranging from grippy to slick. Bob's Area and Salal Point have grippier, more solid stone than much of the neighbourhood. Crags are strung out along a trail: Bob's Area is the largest, with Crag of the 20s, Salal Point Crags and Club Paradiso / The Actual Cave also holding many climbs. Most of the walls suit summer, though some, such as Amazonia, stay wet for a long time.

co_georgetown.blurb: Georgetown sits west of Denver along I-70 at roughly 8,500 feet, and its climbing is strung along the road south of town toward Guanella Pass. Bouldering makes up nearly all of it, concentrated at Guanella Pass among sub-alpine boulders, with a wide spread of grades from V0 into the V10s and V12s and the most problems in the middle range. A few sport and trad lines exist on crags beside the road and the interstate, such as Inaugural Crag and Saxon Rock, and there are a handful of ice and mixed routes. The rock types described for the cliffs and the boulders do not agree, so none is named here.

ct_bald_rock_basin.blurb: Bald Rock Basin lies in Redding, near Danbury, in the western part of Connecticut. It is nearly all bouldering, among the largest collections in the state, with only a few short trad and top-rope lines. Gneiss boulders fill the basin north of Bald Rock, a glacier-shaped peak at about 700 feet; slabs cover its west side and a second boulder field lies below the outcrops on the east. Problems run mostly from V0 to V5, with plenty of easy ones and a small number up to about V8. The Basin Area is the biggest section, followed by Bald Rock itself and the Saddle Area.

ut_utah_hills.blurb: The Utah Hills are desert limestone crags in southwest Utah, a drive from Saint George. Nearly everything is bolted sport climbing, typically one pitch, on solid rock. Grades run from about 5.6 to 5.14, but the weight is in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, with a decent number of 5.13s. Cliffs face every direction, so you can usually chase shade or sun. Fall, spring and winter are the comfortable seasons. Woodbury Road Crags is the largest cluster, and The Diamond, The Simian Complex and Gorilla Cliffs are other busy walls, each holding a few dozen routes.
